blocks.en: Hello, young explorers, and welcome back to Michael's Morning Listening!
Today our first guest is a pumpkin so heavy that it weighs more than a rhinoceros.
Our second guest waited three thousand years inside a dark tomb — a pot of honey!
Big, sweet, and full of surprises.
Let's go!
Meet Bagheera, the heaviest pumpkin in the world!
It weighs one thousand, two hundred and ninety-five kilograms — as heavy as a small car, and heavier than a white rhinoceros.
Around its middle, it measures more than six metres.
Its name comes from a storybook: Bagheera, the black panther in The Jungle Book.
Its grower is Ian, a sixty-five-year-old plant grower from England.
Ian and his twin brother Stuart spent more than fifty years growing giant pumpkins together.
The brothers became champions and even set a world record together.
This year, for the first time, Ian entered the contest alone, determined to beat his own record — and he did!
Growing a champion takes hard work.
For two months, Ian worked up to six hours a day.
On hot days, he gave his plant five hundred and ninety litres of water — enough to fill three bathtubs!
At last, workers lifted Bagheera with a forklift onto a giant scale.
A Guinness judge observed every step and announced: a new world record!
Now Bagheera sits on a farm, and families bring their cameras to take photos beside it.
And when the show ends?
This champion will become dinner — for the cows on the farm!
From one tiny seed to a pumpkin heavier than a rhinoceros: what a champion!
Time for something sweet.
Long ago in Egypt, a king was buried with pots of honey — food for his journey to the next world.
Three thousand years later, explorers opened the tomb and tasted it.
Still good!
How can food stay fresh for three thousand years?
Secret number one: honey is very, very dry.
Bees make it from nectar, the sweet juice inside flowers, fanning their wings like tiny fans to dry it.
Germs need water to live, and inside honey they dry out and die.
Secret number two: honey is a little sour, like lemon juice, and germs hate sour food.
Secret number three: bees add a special enzyme that makes a natural cleaner, stopping germs from growing.
Then the bees seal every cell with wax, like a lid on a tiny jar.
Dry, sour, guarded by a cleaner, and sealed with wax — no wonder honey can wait three thousand years!
Keep the lid closed and the water out, and your honey might wait for you, too.
Here's today's idiom: "a piece of cake." It means something is very easy — as easy as eating a sweet slice of cake.
Listen to little Tom.
His teacher said, "Our class will carve a pumpkin for the autumn festival." Tom smiled and said, "No problem.
Carving a pumpkin is a piece of cake!" Ten minutes later, his pumpkin had a funny face, and Tom won first prize.
But growing a pumpkin like Bagheera?
Ian will tell you: that is NOT a piece of cake!
Let's think about our two stories.
First: if you could grow a giant pumpkin, what would you name it, and what would you do with it?
Second: honey stayed sweet for three thousand years.
If you could save one food for people in the far future, what would you choose?
Talk about it with your family!
That's all for today, young explorers.
Dream big like Ian, work hard like the bees — and see you tomorrow morning!
